prompt.en: Tell me about a technical decision or project that went badly, where you were part of the cause. Name the reasoning error underneath the mistake, and the concrete thing that changed afterwards.
prompt.es: Cuéntame de una decisión técnica o un proyecto que salió mal, donde tú fuiste parte de la causa. Nombra el error de razonamiento debajo del error, y la cosa concreta que cambió después.

criteria.en: Must describe a real failure with a real consequence — time lost, money, an outage, a rebuild, damaged trust. Flag it if the failure is trivially small (reads as evasion) or if it is a disguised strength ('I care too much', 'I work too hard'). Must take first-person ownership: the candidate's own decision or omission must be identifiable, not attributed to changing requirements, another team, or bad luck. Must identify the reasoning error beneath the surface mistake — why they made the wrong call at the time, e.g. an unverified assumption, optimising for the wrong thing, not asking a question — rather than only describing what went wrong mechanically. Must state a concrete, observable change afterwards; 'I learned to communicate better' is unfalsifiable and should be flagged as too vague. Bonus: gives evidence the change persisted in a later situation, quantifies the cost, distinguishes what they knew at the time from what they know now (avoiding hindsight bias), or notes a systemic fix rather than only a personal resolution.
criteria.es: Debe describir un fracaso real con una consecuencia real — tiempo perdido, dinero, una caída, una reconstrucción, confianza dañada. Señálalo si el fracaso es trivialmente chico (se lee como evasión) o si es una fortaleza disfrazada ('me importa demasiado', 'trabajo demasiado'). Debe asumir responsabilidad en primera persona: la decisión u omisión propia del candidato debe ser identificable, no atribuida a requisitos cambiantes, a otro equipo, o a la mala suerte. Debe identificar el error de razonamiento debajo del error superficial — por qué tomó la decisión equivocada en su momento, por ejemplo un supuesto no verificado, optimizar por lo equivocado, no hacer una pregunta — en vez de solo describir mecánicamente qué salió mal. Debe enunciar un cambio concreto y observable posterior; 'aprendí a comunicarme mejor' no se puede falsear y debe señalarse como demasiado vago. Bonus: da evidencia de que el cambio persistió en una situación posterior, cuantifica el costo, distingue lo que sabía entonces de lo que sabe ahora (evitando el sesgo retrospectivo), o nota un arreglo sistémico y no solo una resolución personal.

solution.reference:
I spent six weeks building a configurable rules engine for campaign targeting, and we deleted it four months later.

The context: product had changed the targeting logic twice in the previous quarter, and I concluded it would keep changing. So instead of implementing the current rules, I built a small DSL and an evaluator so that future rule changes would be configuration rather than code. It was, in isolation, decent engineering — tested, documented, and it worked.

My contribution to the failure is straightforward. I decided this alone, in a design I did not write down, and I did not ask the product manager which parts of the targeting logic were actually likely to move. When the requirements did change, both changes needed things the DSL could not express — one needed a lookup against a new data source, the other needed a time window with timezone handling. Both would have been an afternoon in plain code. In the engine they were structural changes to the language. We reverted to hardcoded rules and deleted about 3 000 lines.

The reasoning error underneath was not "I over-engineered". It was that **I predicted the direction of change from the fact of change.** Things had changed twice, so I built for flexibility — but I never checked *which axis* they were likely to change along, and that was one Slack message away. I optimised for a kind of variability I had invented, and the cost was six weeks plus four months of everyone routing around an abstraction that did not fit.

What changed concretely: I now write a one-page design doc for anything longer than about a week, and it has a required section listing the assumptions the design depends on. The point is not the document — it is that writing the assumption "targeting rules will change in ways expressible as boolean predicates" makes it visible to someone who can say "actually, the next change is a new data source". That has since caught two similar mistakes for me before they cost anything, including one where I was about to build a plugin system for a service that turned out to need exactly one plugin, ever.

What I would add in hindsight: I should have shipped the hardcoded version first and let the second change tell me whether an abstraction was warranted. Waiting for the third instance of a pattern before abstracting is a rule I had heard and had not internalised until this.

question.en: How do you handle compensation, scope and level questions?
question.es: ¿Cómo manejas las preguntas de compensación, alcance y nivel?

definition.en:
These are negotiation conversations wearing interview clothes. The main skill is not aggression; it is **not anchoring yourself below where you would have landed**.

**"What are your salary expectations?", asked early.** Answering with a number first is almost always worse for you: if you name below their band, they will not correct you upward. Reasonable deflections, in escalating firmness:

1. "I'd rather understand the scope of the role first — what's the band for this level?" Many companies publish bands or are required by law to share one on request.
2. "I'm looking for a package competitive for a senior backend role in this market. What range did you have budgeted?"
3. If genuinely pushed for a number, give a **range whose bottom you would actually accept**, informed by real data (levels.fyi, Glassdoor, local salary surveys, people you know), and say it is dependent on the total package.

And never give your current salary as an anchor. In many jurisdictions asking is illegal; where it is not, it still anchors your offer to your past employer's budget rather than this role's value.

**Level and scope questions.** "What level do you see yourself at?" is asking whether your self-assessment matches evidence. Answer in terms of **scope of ownership**, not years:
- *Mid*: owns features reliably, needs a defined problem.
- *Senior*: owns a system or a service end to end, takes ambiguous problems and returns scoped ones, is a multiplier through review and mentoring.
- *Staff+*: owns problems that cross teams, and the work is often influence, standards and technical direction rather than code.

Saying "I've been operating at senior scope — I own the ingestion service end to end and lead its on-call — and I'd want the title to reflect that" is concrete and checkable. "I have eight years of experience" is not an argument.

**Levelling down.** If they offer a level below what you targeted, ask a specific question rather than accepting or refusing: "What would you need to see to level someone at senior here?" It is legitimate information, sometimes reveals a genuine gap you can address, and occasionally surfaces that the interview simply did not cover the evidence you have.

**Evaluating the offer.** Base, bonus, equity (and what it is actually worth: what fraction of the company, what stage, what preference stack, what the vesting cliff is), pension, remote policy, on-call expectations and its compensation, learning budget. On-call is the most systematically underweighted item — a role paying 10% more with a one-in-three rota is often a worse offer.

**Tone.** Collaborative, not adversarial: "I'm excited about this role and I want to make the numbers work." Companies expect negotiation and almost never rescind for a polite counter. The most common mistake is not asking at all.

**When you have a competing offer,** mention it factually with the number, never as a threat. "I have another offer at X; I'd prefer this role and I'm hoping we can get closer." That is the sentence.
definition.es:
Estas son conversaciones de negociación vestidas de entrevista. La habilidad principal no es la agresividad; es **no anclarte por debajo de donde habrías caído**.

**"¿Cuáles son tus expectativas salariales?", preguntado temprano.** Responder con un número primero casi siempre es peor para ti: si nombras por debajo de su banda, no te van a corregir hacia arriba. Evasivas razonables, en firmeza creciente:

1. "Prefiero entender primero el alcance del rol — ¿cuál es la banda para este nivel?" Muchas empresas publican bandas o están obligadas por ley a compartirlas si se les pide.
2. "Busco un paquete competitivo para un rol de backend senior en este mercado. ¿Qué rango tenían presupuestado?"
3. Si genuinamente insisten por un número, da un **rango cuyo piso realmente aceptarías**, informado por datos reales (levels.fyi, Glassdoor, encuestas salariales locales, gente que conozcas), y di que depende del paquete total.

Y nunca des tu salario actual como ancla. En muchas jurisdicciones preguntarlo es ilegal; donde no lo es, igual ancla tu oferta al presupuesto de tu empleador anterior en vez de al valor de este rol.

**Preguntas de nivel y alcance.** "¿En qué nivel te ves?" está preguntando si tu autoevaluación coincide con la evidencia. Responde en términos de **alcance de propiedad**, no de años:
- *Mid*: es dueño de funcionalidades de forma confiable, necesita un problema definido.
- *Senior*: es dueño de un sistema o un servicio de punta a punta, toma problemas ambiguos y devuelve problemas acotados, es un multiplicador vía revisión y mentoría.
- *Staff+*: es dueño de problemas que cruzan equipos, y el trabajo suele ser influencia, estándares y dirección técnica más que código.

Decir "vengo operando en alcance senior — soy dueño del servicio de ingesta de punta a punta y lidero su guardia — y querría que el título lo refleje" es concreto y verificable. "Tengo ocho años de experiencia" no es un argumento.

**Si te bajan de nivel.** Si ofrecen un nivel por debajo del que apuntabas, haz una pregunta específica en vez de aceptar o rechazar: "¿Qué necesitarían ver para ubicar a alguien como senior acá?" Es información legítima, a veces revela una brecha real que puedes atender, y ocasionalmente saca a la luz que la entrevista simplemente no cubrió la evidencia que tienes.

**Evaluar la oferta.** Base, bono, equity (y cuánto vale realmente: qué fracción de la empresa, qué etapa, qué estructura de preferencias, cuál es el cliff de vesting), jubilación, política de remoto, expectativas de guardia y su compensación, presupuesto de aprendizaje. La guardia es el ítem más sistemáticamente subvalorado — un rol que paga 10% más con una rotación de uno de cada tres suele ser una peor oferta.

**Tono.** Colaborativo, no adversarial: "Me entusiasma este rol y quiero que los números funcionen." Las empresas esperan negociación y casi nunca retiran una oferta por una contrapropuesta cortés. El error más común es no pedir nada.

**Cuando tienes una oferta competidora,** menciónala con el número y de forma factual, nunca como amenaza. "Tengo otra oferta en X; preferiría este rol y espero que podamos acercarnos." Esa es la frase.

examples.en: A candidate asked for expectations in the first call says "around 70", because that is 10% above their current salary. The band for the role was 85-105. Nobody corrects them upward, and the offer arrives at 74 — a permanent loss anchored by one sentence in a screening call.
examples.es: A un candidato le preguntan sus expectativas en la primera llamada y dice "unos 70", porque es 10% arriba de su salario actual. La banda del rol era 85-105. Nadie lo corrige hacia arriba, y la oferta llega en 74 — una pérdida permanente anclada por una frase en una llamada de filtro.

examples.en: "I have eight years of experience so I should be senior" invites the interviewer to disagree. "I own the payments service end to end, I'm the primary on-call for it, and I mentored two engineers through their first quarter — that's the scope I want the level to reflect" gives them something to verify instead of something to dispute.
examples.es: "Tengo ocho años de experiencia así que debería ser senior" invita al entrevistador a discrepar. "Soy dueño del servicio de pagos de punta a punta, soy el primer contacto de guardia, y mentoreé a dos ingenieros en su primer trimestre — ese es el alcance que quiero que el nivel refleje" les da algo que verificar en vez de algo que disputar.

examples.en: Two offers: one 12% higher base with a one-in-three on-call rota and no compensation for it, one lower with one-in-eight and a day off after a bad night. The second is very often the better offer, and on-call load is the item candidates most reliably forget to ask about before signing.
examples.es: Dos ofertas: una con 12% más de base con una rotación de guardia de uno de cada tres y sin compensación por ella, otra más baja con uno de cada ocho y un día libre después de una mala noche. La segunda muy a menudo es la mejor oferta, y la carga de guardia es el ítem que los candidatos más consistentemente se olvidan de preguntar antes de firmar.

prompt.en: A recruiter asks for your salary expectations in the first screening call. What is the best response?
prompt.es: Un reclutador te pregunta tus expectativas salariales en la primera llamada de filtro. ¿Cuál es la mejor respuesta?

options.en: Give your current salary plus 10%, so the request seems reasonable
options.es: Dar tu salario actual más 10%, para que el pedido parezca razonable

options.en: Name the highest number you can say without laughing, to anchor high
options.es: Nombrar el número más alto que puedas decir sin reírte, para anclar alto

options.en: Refuse to discuss compensation until a written offer exists
options.es: Negarse a hablar de compensación hasta que exista una oferta escrita

options.en: "I'd like to understand the scope of the role first — what range is budgeted for this level?", and give a researched range only if genuinely pushed
options.es: "Me gustaría entender primero el alcance del rol — ¿qué rango tienen presupuestado para este nivel?", y dar un rango investigado solo si insisten de verdad

explanation.en: Whoever names a number first sets the anchor, and if you anchor below their band nobody will correct you upward. Asking for the budgeted range is standard, expected, and in many places legally required to be answered. Anchoring to your current salary ties this offer to your previous employer's budget rather than this role's value. Refusing entirely wastes everyone's time if the bands genuinely do not overlap, and an absurd number ends the conversation.
explanation.es: Quien nombra un número primero fija el ancla, y si te anclas por debajo de su banda nadie te va a corregir hacia arriba. Pedir el rango presupuestado es estándar, esperado, y en muchos lugares hay obligación legal de responderlo. Anclarte a tu salario actual ata esta oferta al presupuesto de tu empleador anterior en vez de al valor de este rol. Negarse por completo hace perder tiempo a todos si las bandas genuinamente no se superponen, y un número absurdo termina la conversación.

prompt.en: You are offered a level below the one you targeted. What is the most useful thing to say?
prompt.es: Te ofrecen un nivel por debajo del que apuntabas. ¿Qué es lo más útil que puedes decir?

options.en: "What would you need to see to level someone as senior here?" — it is real information, may reveal a gap you can address, and sometimes surfaces evidence the interview never asked about
options.es: "¿Qué necesitarían ver para ubicar a alguien como senior acá?" — es información real, puede revelar una brecha que puedes atender, y a veces saca a la luz evidencia que la entrevista nunca preguntó

options.en: Decline immediately — a lower level is not negotiable
options.es: Rechazar de inmediato — un nivel más bajo no es negociable

options.en: Accept it and plan to argue for a promotion in six months
options.es: Aceptarlo y planear pelear un ascenso en seis meses

options.en: Ask for the higher salary band while accepting the lower title
options.es: Pedir la banda salarial más alta aceptando el título más bajo

explanation.en: The question converts a verdict into a conversation, and it is genuinely informative in both directions. Sometimes the answer names a real gap, which tells you what to work on whether or not you take the job. Sometimes it reveals that the interview loop never probed the evidence you had — which is a fair thing to then supply. Accepting quietly plus a private promotion plan is how people end up under-levelled for years, since starting level strongly influences later trajectory.
explanation.es: La pregunta convierte un veredicto en una conversación, y es genuinamente informativa en ambas direcciones. A veces la respuesta nombra una brecha real, lo que te dice en qué trabajar tomes o no el trabajo. A veces revela que el proceso nunca indagó en la evidencia que tenías — que es justo aportar entonces. Aceptar en silencio más un plan privado de ascenso es como la gente termina sub-nivelada por años, ya que el nivel inicial influye fuertemente en la trayectoria posterior.

prompt.en: You receive an offer 15% below your target. You want the job. Write what you would actually say — in an email or a call — to negotiate.
prompt.es: Recibes una oferta 15% por debajo de tu objetivo. Quieres el trabajo. Escribe lo que realmente dirías — en un correo o una llamada — para negociar.

criteria.en: Must be collaborative rather than adversarial in tone, and must express genuine interest in the role — negotiating from enthusiasm is both more effective and more honest than negotiating from leverage alone. Must make a specific, concrete ask rather than a vague 'is there flexibility'; naming a number is the point. Should justify the number with something external: market data, scope of the role, a competing offer stated factually, or the specific value the candidate brings. Should consider the total package, not base alone — equity, signing bonus, on-call compensation, remote policy, learning budget, or an early review are all legitimate levers when base is capped. Must not contain a threat or an ultimatum, and must not cite the candidate's current salary as justification. Bonus: proposes an alternative if base is genuinely fixed (a signing bonus, a six-month review with defined criteria), asks a question rather than only stating a demand, keeps it short, or acknowledges the recruiter's constraints.
criteria.es: Debe tener un tono colaborativo y no adversarial, y debe expresar interés genuino en el rol — negociar desde el entusiasmo es a la vez más efectivo y más honesto que negociar solo desde la palanca. Debe hacer un pedido específico y concreto en vez de un vago '¿hay flexibilidad?'; nombrar un número es el punto. Debería justificar el número con algo externo: datos de mercado, el alcance del rol, una oferta competidora enunciada de forma factual, o el valor específico que aporta el candidato. Debería considerar el paquete total, no solo la base — equity, bono de firma, compensación de guardia, política de remoto, presupuesto de aprendizaje, o una revisión temprana son todas palancas legítimas cuando la base está topada. No debe contener una amenaza ni un ultimátum, y no debe citar el salario actual del candidato como justificación. Bonus: propone una alternativa si la base está genuinamente fija (un bono de firma, una revisión a los seis meses con criterios definidos), hace una pregunta en vez de solo enunciar una exigencia, es breve, o reconoce las restricciones del reclutador.

solution.reference:
Subject: Re: Offer — Senior Backend Engineer

Hi Marta,

Thank you for the offer — I'm genuinely excited about this one. The conversation with the platform team convinced me this is the kind of problem I want to be working on, and I'd like to find a way to make it work.

On compensation: the base is coming in at 85, and based on my research for senior backend roles in this market with this scope — owning a service end to end and being primary on-call for it — I've been targeting 98. I also have an offer in hand at 96, though I'd genuinely prefer this role.

Would you be able to get to 95 on base? If the band is firm at this level, I'm open to other ways of closing the gap — a signing bonus, additional equity, or a documented six-month review with agreed criteria for moving to the next band would all work for me.

One more thing I'd like to understand before deciding: what does the on-call rota look like for this team, and is there compensation or time off associated with it? That genuinely factors into how I compare the two offers.

Happy to jump on a call if that's easier.

Best,
Alex

---

Why it is written this way: it opens with real enthusiasm rather than leverage, so the recruiter is working *with* the candidate rather than defending a position. It names a specific number instead of asking whether there is flexibility, which is the single most common way candidates leave money on the table. The competing offer appears as a fact, not a threat, and is immediately followed by a stated preference for this role. It offers alternative levers in case base is genuinely capped, which makes it easy to say yes to something. And it asks about on-call — the item most systematically forgotten before signing, and one that can matter more than the 10% under discussion. Nowhere does it mention the candidate's current salary, which would anchor this offer to a previous employer's budget rather than to this role's value.

question.en: What should you ask them, and what does each question reveal?
question.es: ¿Qué deberías preguntarles a ellos, y qué revela cada pregunta?

definition.en:
"Do you have any questions for us?" is not a formality. It is the last five minutes and it is still being scored — and it is also the only part of the process where **you** are evaluating **them**, which most candidates forget entirely.

**Questions that reveal how the team actually works:**
- *"Walk me through what happened with the last production incident."* The single highest-information question available. You learn whether they have monitoring, whether postmortems are blameless, whether follow-up work actually ships, and how they talk about mistakes — all from one answer.
- *"How does code get from a laptop to production? How long does that take?"* Reveals CI/CD maturity, test culture, review process, and release fear.
- *"What is on-call like? How often, and what happened the last time someone was paged at night?"* The specific version is the useful one; "we have on-call" tells you nothing.
- *"What does the team spend time on that it wishes it did not?"* Surfaces toil, tech debt and process pain that no one volunteers.

**Questions that reveal the role's reality:**
- *"What would the first ninety days look like, and what would success look like at the end of them?"* If they cannot answer concretely, the role may not be well defined — which is a genuine risk.
- *"Why is this position open?"* Growth, backfill, or churn are three very different situations.
- *"What is the biggest technical decision the team is facing right now?"* You get a real problem to reason about, and it often turns into the best conversation of the interview.

**Questions that reveal growth and stability:**
- *"How are promotions decided here, and can you tell me about someone who was promoted recently?"* The second half is what makes it useful.
- *"What is the tenure of the team? Has anyone left recently, and why?"*
- *"How does the team decide what to work on?"*

**Ask the right person.** An engineer can answer about on-call, code review and the last incident. A hiring manager can answer about roadmap, team growth and promotion. A recruiter can answer about process and compensation bands. Asking a recruiter about deployment frequency wastes your best question.

**Avoid:** anything answerable from the careers page; "what does a typical day look like" (generic, generic answer); and — early on — questions that are only about what you receive (holiday, remote days, perks) before any about the work itself. Those are legitimate and you should absolutely ask them, but at offer stage.

**Listen to the answer, not just the fact that you asked.** Hesitation on "why is this position open" or a vague answer on the last incident is real data. And prepare more questions than you need — several will be answered during the conversation, and having nothing left is a bad final impression.
definition.es:
"¿Tienes alguna pregunta para nosotros?" no es una formalidad. Son los últimos cinco minutos y se siguen calificando — y es además la única parte del proceso donde **tú** los evalúas a **ellos**, algo que la mayoría de los candidatos olvida por completo.

**Preguntas que revelan cómo funciona el equipo de verdad:**
- *"Cuéntame qué pasó en el último incidente de producción."* La pregunta de mayor información disponible. Aprendes si tienen monitoreo, si los postmortems son sin culpables, si el trabajo de seguimiento realmente se entrega, y cómo hablan de los errores — todo de una sola respuesta.
- *"¿Cómo llega el código de una laptop a producción? ¿Cuánto tarda eso?"* Revela madurez de CI/CD, cultura de tests, proceso de revisión, y miedo a desplegar.
- *"¿Cómo es la guardia? ¿Con qué frecuencia, y qué pasó la última vez que alguien recibió una alerta de noche?"* La versión específica es la útil; "tenemos guardia" no te dice nada.
- *"¿En qué gasta tiempo el equipo que preferiría no gastar?"* Saca a la luz trabajo repetitivo, deuda técnica y dolores de proceso que nadie ofrece por su cuenta.

**Preguntas que revelan la realidad del rol:**
- *"¿Cómo serían los primeros noventa días, y cómo se vería el éxito al final de ellos?"* Si no pueden responder concretamente, el rol puede no estar bien definido — que es un riesgo genuino.
- *"¿Por qué está abierta esta posición?"* Crecimiento, reemplazo o rotación son tres situaciones muy distintas.
- *"¿Cuál es la decisión técnica más grande que el equipo está enfrentando ahora?"* Obtienes un problema real sobre el que razonar, y a menudo se convierte en la mejor conversación de la entrevista.

**Preguntas que revelan crecimiento y estabilidad:**
- *"¿Cómo se deciden los ascensos acá, y me pueden contar de alguien que ascendió recientemente?"* La segunda mitad es lo que la vuelve útil.
- *"¿Cuál es la antigüedad del equipo? ¿Se fue alguien recientemente, y por qué?"*
- *"¿Cómo decide el equipo en qué trabajar?"*

**Pregúntale a la persona correcta.** Un ingeniero puede responder sobre guardia, revisión de código y el último incidente. Un hiring manager puede responder sobre roadmap, crecimiento del equipo y ascensos. Un reclutador puede responder sobre el proceso y las bandas de compensación. Preguntarle a un reclutador por la frecuencia de despliegue desperdicia tu mejor pregunta.

**Evita:** cualquier cosa contestable desde la página de empleos; "¿cómo es un día típico?" (genérica, respuesta genérica); y — temprano en el proceso — preguntas que son solo sobre lo que recibes (vacaciones, días de remoto, beneficios) antes de cualquiera sobre el trabajo en sí. Son legítimas y absolutamente debes preguntarlas, pero en la etapa de oferta.

**Escucha la respuesta, no solo el hecho de haber preguntado.** Una vacilación ante "¿por qué está abierta esta posición?" o una respuesta vaga sobre el último incidente son datos reales. Y prepara más preguntas de las que necesitas — varias se van a responder durante la conversación, y quedarte sin ninguna es una mala impresión final.

examples.en: "Tell me about the last production incident" gets an answer like: "a config change took down search for 20 minutes, we found it through customer reports, and the postmortem action items are still open." That single answer told the candidate there is no alerting on a user-facing path and postmortem follow-through is weak — information no careers page contains.
examples.es: "Cuéntame del último incidente de producción" obtiene una respuesta como: "un cambio de configuración tiró la búsqueda 20 minutos, nos enteramos por reportes de clientes, y las acciones del postmortem siguen abiertas." Esa sola respuesta le dijo al candidato que no hay alertas en un camino de cara al usuario y que el seguimiento de postmortems es débil — información que ninguna página de empleos contiene.

examples.en: "How long from merge to production?" answered as "we release every two weeks and it's a bit of a process" versus "about twelve minutes, and anyone can deploy" describes two entirely different jobs, whatever the job description said.
examples.es: "¿Cuánto pasa de un merge a producción?" respondido como "lanzamos cada dos semanas y es un poco un proceso" contra "unos doce minutos, y cualquiera puede desplegar" describe dos trabajos completamente distintos, diga lo que diga la descripción del puesto.

examples.en: Asked "why is this position open?", an interviewer hesitates and says "the last person moved on". Following up gently — "how long were they in the role?" — is entirely fair, and "about five months" is a data point worth having before signing.
examples.es: Ante "¿por qué está abierta esta posición?", un entrevistador vacila y dice "la última persona siguió su camino". Repreguntar con suavidad — "¿cuánto tiempo estuvo en el rol?" — es completamente justo, y "unos cinco meses" es un dato que conviene tener antes de firmar.

prompt.en: Write the three questions you would ask a senior engineer on the team you would be joining, and for each one, say what you would learn from the answer — including what a *bad* answer would look like.

criteria.en: Must give exactly three questions, each appropriate for an engineer rather than a recruiter or HR — questions about remote policy, holiday, headcount or compensation bands are misdirected here and should be flagged. Each question must be paired with a stated rationale for what it reveals, and crucially with what a bad answer would look like; omitting the bad-answer half is the most likely gap and should be called out, since it is what turns asking into evaluating. Questions should be specific and concrete rather than generic ('what's a typical day', 'what's the culture like' produce generic answers). Strong choices include the last production incident, merge-to-production time and who can deploy, on-call reality, what the team wishes it did not spend time on, the biggest current technical decision, or why the position is open. Bonus: notes that the candidate is evaluating the company too, mentions listening to hesitation or vagueness as data, prepares more questions than needed because some get answered during the conversation, or explains how a specific bad answer would change their decision.
criteria.es: Debe dar exactamente tres preguntas, cada una apropiada para un ingeniero y no para un reclutador o RRHH — preguntas sobre política de remoto, vacaciones, cantidad de gente o bandas de compensación están mal dirigidas acá y deben señalarse. Cada pregunta debe ir acompañada de una justificación de qué revela, y fundamentalmente de cómo se vería una mala respuesta; omitir la mitad de la mala respuesta es la brecha más probable y debe señalarse, ya que es lo que convierte el preguntar en evaluar. Las preguntas deben ser específicas y concretas en vez de genéricas ('cómo es un día típico', 'cómo es la cultura' producen respuestas genéricas). Buenas elecciones incluyen el último incidente de producción, el tiempo de merge a producción y quién puede desplegar, la realidad de la guardia, en qué preferiría el equipo no gastar tiempo, la decisión técnica más grande actual, o por qué está abierta la posición. Bonus: nota que el candidato también está evaluando a la empresa, menciona escuchar la vacilación o la vaguedad como dato, prepara más preguntas de las necesarias porque algunas se responden en la conversación, o explica cómo una mala respuesta concreta cambiaría su decisión.

solution.reference:
**1. "Walk me through the last production incident — how did you find out, and what changed afterwards?"**

What I learn: whether they have real alerting on user-facing paths, whether postmortems are blameless, and — the part most teams fail — whether the action items actually shipped. It is the highest-information question I can ask an engineer, because it is a concrete story rather than a description of how they would like to work.

A bad answer: "a customer emailed support, and honestly the postmortem doc is still open from March." That tells me detection depends on users and that follow-up work loses to feature work. Also bad in a different way: "we don't really have incidents" — either they are not looking, or I am about to be the person who discovers that.

**2. "How long does it take for a merged pull request to reach production, and who is allowed to deploy?"**

What I learn: CI/CD maturity, test confidence, and how much fear surrounds a release. Deploy frequency is the best single proxy for engineering health I know, because a team that deploys many times a day has necessarily solved testing, review, rollback and observability.

A bad answer: "we release every two weeks and the release manager coordinates it." Not disqualifying, but it means slow feedback loops and large risky batches, and I would want to know whether they see that as a problem they are working on or as simply how things are. The worse version is "it depends — sometimes a release takes a few days if something goes wrong", which suggests deploys are not reliably reversible.

**3. "What does the team spend time on that it wishes it did not?"**

What I learn: the toil, the tech debt, and the process pain that nobody volunteers in an interview. It is deliberately phrased to give permission to complain, and the honesty of the answer is itself a signal about how safe it is to say critical things on this team.

A bad answer: "nothing really, things run pretty smoothly." Every team has toil. Either they are not being candid with me, or they have stopped noticing — and both mean I will find out after I join. A *good* bad answer, which I would actually be encouraged by, is a specific complaint plus what they are doing about it: "flaky tests eat a day a week, and we've got a working group on it that's halved it since January."

I would prepare five or six of these rather than three, because two or three usually get answered during the conversation. And I would pay as much attention to hesitation as to content — if "why is this position open" produces a pause, that pause is the answer.

question.en: How do you open with "tell me about yourself"?

definition.en:
It is the first question in almost every interview, it is entirely predictable, and it is the one most people improvise. It sets the frame for the next forty-five minutes: a good answer makes the interviewer ask about the thing you want to talk about.

**The structure: Now → Then → Why here.** Ninety seconds, not five minutes.

1. **Now (20 s).** What you do currently, with scope. "I'm a backend engineer at a fintech, where I own the payments ingestion service — about 8 000 events a second — and I'm primary on-call for it." Scope and a number, immediately.
2. **Then (40 s).** The path that led here, told as a **trajectory, not a resume**. Two or three moves, each with a reason. "I started in full-stack at an agency, moved to backend because I found the data modelling problems more interesting, and over the last three years I've specialised in high-throughput systems." Skip jobs that do not serve the story — they can read the CV.
3. **Why here (20 s).** Something specific about *this* role or company. "I'm interested in this role because you're solving the same ingestion problems at a scale I haven't worked at, and the engineering blog post about your migration off Kafka was the most honest thing I've read about that trade-off." Generic enthusiasm is worse than none — it signals you are running the same script at five companies.
4. **Optionally, hand them a thread.** End with a hook you would like to be asked about: "...and most recently I've been working on getting our p99 under 200 ms, which turned out to be mostly a connection pooling problem." Interviewers frequently follow the last thing you said.

**What to leave out:** where you were born, your degree unless it is recent or relevant, hobbies unless they connect, and a chronological walk through every job since 2014. The chronological retelling is the single most common version and the least effective, because it forces the interviewer to work out what matters.

**Calibrate to the interviewer.** With a recruiter, lean on scope, motivation and trajectory. With an engineer, get to the technical specifics faster. With a hiring manager, emphasise ownership and impact.

**Practise it out loud, once or twice, not twenty times.** It should sound prepared but not recited — a memorised paragraph delivered at speed is worse than a slightly rough answer with real content in it. And time it: most people's first attempt runs to three or four minutes, which spends a tenth of the interview before any question has been asked.
definition.es:
Es la primera pregunta de casi toda entrevista, es completamente predecible, y es la que la mayoría improvisa. Fija el marco para los siguientes cuarenta y cinco minutos: una buena respuesta hace que el entrevistador pregunte por lo que tú quieres hablar.

**La estructura: Ahora → Antes → Por qué acá.** Noventa segundos, no cinco minutos.

1. **Ahora (20 s).** Qué haces actualmente, con alcance. "Soy ingeniero backend en una fintech, donde soy dueño del servicio de ingesta de pagos — unos 8 000 eventos por segundo — y soy el primer contacto de guardia." Alcance y un número, de inmediato.
2. **Antes (40 s).** El camino que te trajo acá, contado como una **trayectoria, no un currículum**. Dos o tres movimientos, cada uno con una razón. "Empecé en full-stack en una agencia, me moví a backend porque los problemas de modelado de datos me parecían más interesantes, y en los últimos tres años me especialicé en sistemas de alto throughput." Salta los trabajos que no sirven a la historia — pueden leer el CV.
3. **Por qué acá (20 s).** Algo específico de *este* rol o empresa. "Me interesa este rol porque están resolviendo los mismos problemas de ingesta a una escala en la que no trabajé, y el post del blog de ingeniería sobre su migración fuera de Kafka fue lo más honesto que leí sobre ese trade-off." El entusiasmo genérico es peor que ninguno — señala que estás corriendo el mismo guion en cinco empresas.
4. **Opcionalmente, dales un hilo.** Termina con un gancho sobre el que te gustaría que te preguntaran: "...y últimamente estuve trabajando en bajar nuestro p99 de 200 ms, que resultó ser mayormente un problema de pooling de conexiones." Los entrevistadores frecuentemente siguen lo último que dijiste.

**Qué dejar afuera:** dónde naciste, tu título salvo que sea reciente o relevante, hobbies salvo que conecten, y un recorrido cronológico por cada trabajo desde 2014. El recuento cronológico es la versión más común y la menos efectiva, porque obliga al entrevistador a deducir qué importa.

**Calibra según el entrevistador.** Con un reclutador, apóyate en alcance, motivación y trayectoria. Con un ingeniero, llega a lo técnico más rápido. Con un hiring manager, enfatiza propiedad e impacto.

**Practícala en voz alta, una o dos veces, no veinte.** Debe sonar preparada pero no recitada — un párrafo memorizado dicho a toda velocidad es peor que una respuesta un poco áspera con contenido real. Y tómale el tiempo: el primer intento de la mayoría se va a tres o cuatro minutos, lo que gasta una décima parte de la entrevista antes de que se haya hecho ninguna pregunta.

examples.en: "I graduated in 2016, then I was at company A for two years doing mostly frontend, then company B where I did some backend and some DevOps, then company C..." — four minutes in, the interviewer has no idea what this person is good at or wants. The chronology is available on the CV; the trajectory is not.
examples.es: "Me recibí en 2016, después estuve en la empresa A dos años haciendo mayormente frontend, después en la empresa B donde hice algo de backend y algo de DevOps, después en la empresa C..." — a los cuatro minutos, el entrevistador no tiene idea en qué es bueno ni qué quiere esta persona. La cronología está en el CV; la trayectoria no.

examples.en: Ending with "...and most recently I've been working on getting our p99 under 200 ms, which turned out to be a connection pooling problem rather than a query problem" reliably produces "tell me about that" as the next question — which is a conversation the candidate chose and is prepared for.
examples.es: Terminar con "...y últimamente estuve trabajando en bajar nuestro p99 de 200 ms, que resultó ser un problema de pooling de conexiones y no de consultas" produce confiablemente "cuéntame de eso" como siguiente pregunta — que es una conversación que el candidato eligió y para la que está preparado.

examples.en: "I'm excited about your company's mission and culture of innovation" is indistinguishable from what every other candidate said, and interviewers hear it as a template. "Your post about moving off Kafka matched a decision we got wrong last year" cannot have been said by anyone who did not do the reading.
examples.es: "Me entusiasma la misión de su empresa y su cultura de innovación" es indistinguible de lo que dijo cualquier otro candidato, y los entrevistadores lo escuchan como una plantilla. "Su post sobre migrar fuera de Kafka coincide con una decisión que nosotros hicimos mal el año pasado" no lo pudo haber dicho nadie que no hiciera la lectura.

prompt.en: Write your own 90-second answer to "tell me about yourself", for a senior backend role you would actually want. Use Now → Then → Why here, and end with a hook you would like to be asked about.
prompt.es: Escribe tu propia respuesta de 90 segundos a "cuéntame de ti", para un rol senior de backend que realmente quisieras. Usa Ahora → Antes → Por qué acá, y termina con un gancho sobre el que te gustaría que preguntaran.

criteria.en: Must follow the Now → Then → Why here structure and be roughly 90 seconds of speech — if it reads as three or four minutes, flag the length, since running long is the most common failure. 'Now' should state current scope concretely, ideally with a number or a named system rather than a job title alone. 'Then' must be a trajectory with reasons for the moves, not a chronological list of employers; a resume recital is the key weakness to call out. 'Why here' must be specific to a role or company — generic enthusiasm about 'mission' or 'culture of innovation' should be flagged as interchangeable with every other candidate's answer. Should end with a hook: a concrete recent piece of work the candidate would like to be asked about. Bonus: leaves out irrelevant biography (birthplace, unrelated degree, full job history), calibrates the technical depth to the audience, or picks a hook that sets up a story they are genuinely prepared to tell in STAR form.
criteria.es: Debe seguir la estructura Ahora → Antes → Por qué acá y ser aproximadamente 90 segundos de habla — si se lee como tres o cuatro minutos, señala el largo, ya que excederse es el fallo más común. 'Ahora' debe enunciar el alcance actual de forma concreta, idealmente con un número o un sistema nombrado y no solo un título de puesto. 'Antes' debe ser una trayectoria con razones para los movimientos, no una lista cronológica de empleadores; recitar el currículum es la debilidad clave a señalar. 'Por qué acá' debe ser específico de un rol o empresa — el entusiasmo genérico sobre la 'misión' o la 'cultura de innovación' debe señalarse como intercambiable con la respuesta de cualquier otro candidato. Debería terminar con un gancho: un trabajo reciente concreto sobre el que al candidato le gustaría que preguntaran. Bonus: deja afuera biografía irrelevante (lugar de nacimiento, título no relacionado, historial laboral completo), calibra la profundidad técnica a la audiencia, o elige un gancho que prepare una historia que genuinamente puede contar en formato STAR.

solution.reference:
**Now.** I'm a backend engineer at a payments company, where I own our event ingestion service end to end — it handles around 8 000 events a second at peak, and I'm the primary on-call for it. Day to day that's a mix of Python and Postgres, with a fair amount of time in query plans and capacity planning.

**Then.** I started in full-stack at an agency, which was a good way to see a lot of codebases quickly but meant I was always shallow. I moved to a product company specifically to go deeper on the backend, because the problems I kept finding interesting were the data modelling ones rather than the interface ones. Over the last three years that's narrowed further into high-throughput systems — I've spent most of my time on the write path, on the database side of latency, and on the operational reality of running something that cannot go down during business hours.

**Why here.** I'm interested in this role because you're solving the same ingestion problems an order of magnitude above where I've worked, and because of the engineering blog post about moving off Kafka — it's the most honest write-up of that trade-off I've read, including the parts where it did not work out. We made close to the opposite decision last year and I'd like to work somewhere that writes that kind of thing down.

**Hook.** The thing I've spent most of this quarter on is getting our p99 under 200 ms, which I assumed would be a query optimisation problem and turned out to be almost entirely connection pooling — I'd be happy to go into that if it's useful.

---

Why it is shaped this way: the first sentence gives scope and a number, so the interviewer immediately knows what level of problem I work on. The middle is a trajectory with *reasons* — full-stack to backend because of the kind of problem, backend to high-throughput because of where that led — rather than a list of employers with dates, which are already on the CV. The 'why here' cites something specific enough that I could not have said it to another company. And the hook hands them a thread I want to be pulled, which is the p99 story I have prepared in STAR form.

prompt.en: An interviewer asks: "tell me about a time you disagreed with a technical decision and lost." Explain what a strong answer contains, and what the interviewer is actually assessing.
prompt.es: Un entrevistador pregunta: "cuéntame de una vez que discrepaste con una decisión técnica y perdiste." Explica qué contiene una respuesta fuerte, y qué está evaluando realmente el entrevistador.

criteria.en: Must identify that the interviewer is assessing two things simultaneously: whether the candidate holds and argues technical positions with evidence, and whether they can commit fully to a decision that went against them (disagree and commit). Must say a strong answer frames the disagreement technically rather than as a personality conflict, steelmans the other side's reasoning, describes converting opinion into evidence (a prototype, benchmark, load test, written doc, or third opinion) rather than persuasion by seniority, and states honestly what happened. Must cover what the candidate did after losing: implementing the chosen approach properly rather than half-heartedly, ideally with the concern recorded somewhere. Should note that disparaging the other person is disqualifying, and that an answer where the candidate turned out to be wrong is often stronger because it shows they can update. Bonus: mentions recording a falsifiable trigger so the concern becomes useful rather than an I-told-you-so, notes that sabotage-by-compliance is a real failure mode interviewers screen for, or distinguishes reversible from irreversible decisions when discussing escalation.
criteria.es: Debe identificar que el entrevistador evalúa dos cosas a la vez: si el candidato sostiene y argumenta posiciones técnicas con evidencia, y si puede comprometerse por completo con una decisión que fue en su contra (discrepar y comprometerse). Debe decir que una respuesta fuerte encuadra el desacuerdo técnicamente y no como conflicto de personalidad, presenta la mejor versión del razonamiento del otro lado, describe convertir opinión en evidencia (un prototipo, benchmark, prueba de carga, documento escrito, o una tercera opinión) en vez de persuasión por antigüedad, y enuncia honestamente qué pasó. Debe cubrir qué hizo el candidato después de perder: implementar el enfoque elegido bien y no a medias, idealmente con la preocupación registrada en algún lado. Debería notar que hablar mal de la otra persona es descalificante, y que una respuesta donde el candidato resultó estar equivocado suele ser más fuerte porque muestra que puede actualizar su posición. Bonus: menciona registrar un disparador falseable para que la preocupación sea útil en vez de un te-lo-dije, nota que el sabotaje por cumplimiento es un modo de fallo real que los entrevistadores filtran, o distingue decisiones reversibles de irreversibles al hablar de escalar.

solution.reference:
The interviewer is assessing two things at once, and they are in tension — which is why the question is useful.

The first is whether you have technical conviction: do you form positions, and do you argue for them with something better than preference? A candidate who says they never disagree reads as either having no opinions or being willing to watch a bad decision ship silently. Neither is what a senior hire looks like.

The second is whether you can lose well. A technically strong engineer who cannot commit to a decision that went against them is a net negative on a team, because every settled question stays open. The phrase 'and lost' in the question is deliberate: they want to see disagree-and-commit specifically.

A strong answer contains five things.

It frames the disagreement as technical, not personal — 'we disagreed about whether to introduce a queue', not 'my lead was stubborn'. Disparaging a named former colleague is close to disqualifying, because the interviewer only has your account and what they are actually learning is how you talk about people who are not in the room.

It steelmans the other position: states their reasoning as well as they would have. This is the strongest single move available, because it proves you understood the argument rather than talked past it. If their argument was 'we are three people and every stateful system is on-call burden', say that, and say it as a good argument.

It describes how you tried to resolve it, and the good answers all involve converting opinion into evidence — a prototype, a load test, a written design doc, a third perspective. Not persuasion by persistence or seniority.

It states the outcome honestly. And notably, an answer where you turned out to be *wrong* is often stronger than one where you were right, because updating on evidence is exactly the behaviour being screened for.

Finally, it says what you did next. The good version is: record the concern somewhere durable — ideally with a falsifiable trigger, like 'this breaks down past about 400 concurrent workers' — and then implement their approach properly. The trigger is what turns the concern into something useful later rather than an I-told-you-so. The bad versions are all forms of not committing: implementing it minimally so the failure is obvious, leaving passive-aggressive comments in the code, or relitigating the decision in the next three team meetings. Interviewers know sabotage-by-compliance is a real failure mode and they are listening for it.

A good closing beat is what you would do differently — usually raising it earlier, in writing, or with data instead of instinct.
